title: Induction training for a new carer: day one to day seven. Did any of it go in?
meta_title: Induction Training for Care Staff: Day 1 to 7 | CareStreamAI
meta_description: A new starter reads policies all week. Give your induction training a question after each one, so by day seven you know what went in. Try it free.

intro.heading: You have run the week. Now you need to know it landed.
intro.sub: A scenario we see in many care settings.
intro.paragraph: Amira starts on a Monday. The manager welcomes her, shows her round and hands her a folder. Over the week she reads the safeguarding policy, the medication policy, the fire policy and a dozen more, and she shadows two experienced carers. Each policy gets a tick. By Friday the folder is full and everyone is pleased. On the following Monday, day seven, the manager is asked whether Amira is ready to work with more independence. There is a lot of paper and no real answer, because nobody has asked her a single question.

trail.text: Amira is welcomed, shown round and given her login for the Staff Hub.
She shadows two carers and reads the safeguarding and fire policies.
She reads medication, infection control and the rest. Every one is ticked.
Nobody has asked her anything yet. The ticks look the same whether she read or skimmed.

trail.when: What the ticks do not show
trail.text: Whether she knows who the safeguarding lead is, or what to do if a resident falls.
She is reluctant to say what she did not follow. New starters rarely do.
A full folder. Nothing showing what went in.
“How do you know new staff understood their induction?” Ticks are not an answer.

trail_close: The week was never the problem. The gap is between reading and knowing. Here is how CareStream adds a question after each policy, so day seven has an answer.

why.heading: A tick shows a policy was opened, not that it was understood
why.sub: By day seven you need more than a full folder. You need to know where the gaps are while there is still time to close them.

cards.title: New starters seldom say they are lost
cards.body: Everything is new and everyone seems busy. A new carer will nod and move on, so a quiet week can hide a lot of questions nobody asked.

cards.title: Reading is not the same as knowing
cards.body: A policy can be marked as read in a few seconds. A single question after it shows whether the key point stuck, and that is the point of a knowledge check.

cards.title: The gap shows up later, on the floor
cards.body: If it is not found in week one, it is found when something goes wrong with a resident. Finding it on day four costs a short lesson, not an incident.

talk.heading: The questions managers ask, and how CareStream answers them
talk.sub: Read this as a conversation. The questions are the ones we hear most.

items.q: We already have a good induction. Why add anything?
items.a: You would not replace it. Keep the welcome, the tour and the shadow shifts. CareStream adds a question after each policy, so that induction for new staff includes a check on what was understood and not only what was read.

items.q: Where do the induction questions come from?
items.a: You adopt a ready made flow for the role, and CareStream matches each step to your own policies and rewrites the multiple choice questions to your wording. You can edit the flow after that. Where your policies do not cover a point, the ready made question stays as it is.

items.q: How does a new starter get onto the flow?
items.a: When you add someone with the staff type New starter, they are enrolled automatically in the flows that match their job role. You can also enrol people yourself, with an optional due date, and they are emailed.

items.q: What happens when a new starter gets a question wrong?
items.a: In an induction they have to retry it. The wrong answer also goes into their Follow-up tab in the Staff Hub, and they get an email, at most once a day. They choose Learn & retry, a short lesson then a fresh question, or Just retry the same one. You do not have to chase it.

items.q: Do I get told every time someone answers wrongly?
items.a: No. Nothing alerts you for each wrong answer. You see the picture in the induction progress matrix, on the staff record and in Knowledge gaps, plus a Monday digest email. That keeps the week calm for you and for the new starter.

items.q: Does the manager sign off the induction in CareStream?
items.a: Not inside an induction flow. There is no signature step. A policy step is completed when the starter marks it as read, and a question step when they answer correctly. Your own observation and sign off for practical skills stays with you.

items.q: What if someone has not even started?
items.a: The staff record carries a flag, Induction not started after 7+ days, and an overdue flag when a due date passes. So a quiet week does not turn into a quiet month.

limits.heading: A check on understanding, not a replacement for your welcome

cards.title: It does not replace shadowing or observation
cards.body: Learning how to help someone move, or how your residents like their tea, still needs an experienced colleague beside them. A flow checks understanding. It does not watch practice.

cards.title: There is no manager sign off step in an induction flow
cards.body: A flow has two step types, read a policy and answer a question. There is no signature step. Keep your own sign off for practical competence.

cards.title: It does not alert you to each wrong answer
cards.body: Gaps reach you through the progress matrix, the staff record, Knowledge gaps and the Monday digest, not as a message each time. Translation and adhoc training are on the paid plans only.

items.q: What should induction training for care staff include?
items.a: Your own welcome, a tour, shadow shifts and the policies that matter most in the first week, such as safeguarding, medication and fire. The Skills for Care Care Certificate standards are designed for people new to care and can inform what an induction covers.

items.q: What is a good staff induction checklist?
items.a: Keep it short: welcome and tour, login to the Staff Hub, key policies read, a question after each, a shadow shift with someone experienced, and a review conversation. A flow in CareStream covers the policies and questions part of that staff induction checklist.

items.q: What are good induction questions for new starters?
items.a: Ask what they would actually do: who they tell about a concern, what they do after a fall, how they report a medication error. Multiple choice induction questions built from your own policies check that, and a wrong answer becomes a short lesson.

items.q: How long should an induction programme take?
items.a: It depends on the role and the service. Many homes plan the first week closely and carry on over several weeks. See how long the Care Certificate takes for a guide.

items.q: Can I use the same flow for every role?
items.a: You can adopt a ready made flow per role, such as care assistant or cleaner, and a flow with no roles applies to everyone. New starters are enrolled in the flows that match their job role.

items.q: What if a new starter is not confident in English?
items.a: Induction content can be opened in their own language once your admin sets it, which is part of the paid plans. See the multilingual Staff Hub. The emails stay in English.

items.q: Will an inspector accept this as evidence of induction?
items.a: The regulations say staff must receive the support and training they need for their duties. See Regulation 18 on staffing. A record of questions, results and follow up shows more than a tick. It sits with the rest of your CQC evidence.

items.q: Is a knowledge check enough to show someone is competent?
items.a: No. A knowledge check shows understanding. Competence in practical skills still needs observation by a competent person, and your own sign off. See staff questions for inspection for what staff may be asked.

guide.heading: A practical way to run the first week
guide.lede: Employee induction does not end when the folder is full. A week of reading is a good start. The part that tells you something is what happens when you ask the new starter a question.

sections.h3: Plan the week around questions, not just reading
paragraphs: Put a question straight after each important policy, while it is fresh. Keep the questions about what the starter would do, not what the policy says. Spread the reading across the week so the first day is not a wall of paper, and keep a time in the diary on day seven to talk it through together. If a question has been missed, that conversation is easier to have in week one than in month three.

sections.h3: Five checks that fit a busy week
checklist: Day one: welcome, tour, Staff Hub login and a named person to ask.
Days two to five: read each policy and answer the question that follows it.
Whenever an answer is wrong: they open the short lesson, then answer a fresh question.
Day six: look at the induction progress and any follow up still open.
Day seven: a short conversation, plus practical observation for skills that need it.

guide.note: For the inspector. Keep the policies read, the questions answered and the follow up together on the staff record, so you can show understanding as well as attendance.
